analysis.one_liner: Requires federal agencies to justify major regulations with cost-benefit analysis and risk assessment before issuing them.
analysis.headline: A Senate committee approved this regulatory cost-benefit bill with a bipartisan 24-cosponsor base in May 1998, but it sat on the Senate calendar and never received a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required federal agencies to prepare detailed cost-benefit and risk analyses for any 'major rule' — one costing the economy $100 million a year or more — and to explain why they chose a rule over cheaper alternatives. It would have suspended statutory and court-ordered rulemaking deadlines for up to two years, created advisory committees to recommend old rules for review or repeal, and let courts consider the new analyses when judging whether rules are arbitrary. It also would have opened to the public the written record of White House budget-office review of pending rules, and it explicitly carved out banking, securities, and product-approval rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries regulated by major federal rules. They would gain mandatory consideration of cheaper 'flexible' alternatives, a two-year breathing spell on rule deadlines, formal peer review that delays each analysis, five-year review panels that can recommend old rules for repeal, and a new body of analysis they could cite when challenging rules in court.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated industries facing major federal rules

how_it_helps.text: Agencies would have to prepare cost-benefit analyses, risk assessments, and independent peer review for every major rule before proposing it, and explain any choice of a rule whose benefits do not justify its costs.

All statutory deadlines requiring agencies to issue major rules during the bill's first two years would be suspended until the analysis was done or up to six months past the deadline, and courts could extend litigated deadlines on the government's request.

Each agency that issued a major rule in the prior decade would have to create an outside advisory committee to list old rules for review, and agencies would give deference to recommendations aimed at substantially increasing net benefits, including through repeal.

The Office of Management and Budget would have to disclose to the public all written communications about pending rules between reviewers and outside parties, plus explanations of every review action — a transparency measure aimed at back-channel influence.

analysis.who_pays: People who depend on federal health, safety, and environmental protections. The added analyses, peer review, and deadline suspensions would slow the issuance of major protective rules, and courts would weigh the cost-benefit record when deciding whether a rule survives challenge.
analysis.who_pays_short: People relying on federal health and safety rules

drawbacks.text: The bill would suspend statutory and court-ordered deadlines for major rules for up to two years, delaying rules that Congress or courts had already scheduled to protect the public.

By making the cost-benefit analysis and risk assessment part of the record courts use to judge whether a rule is 'arbitrary or capricious,' the bill would give regulated parties new grounds to attack rules whose benefits are real but hard to quantify in dollars.

The bill exempts rules on banking, securities markets, and the approval of products for market entry, so the industries most centrally tied to the 1990s financial system would be outside the new analysis regime entirely.

The analytical and reporting burden falls on agency staff, diverting resources from enforcement and rulewriting toward paperwork that industry reviewers, not the public, are best positioned to litigate over.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The version the committee reported was a compromise: it preserved existing substantive legal standards for rules, required analysis of protections for sensitive subpopulations, and added real transparency to White House regulatory review. But its core mechanism — mandatory cost-benefit analysis with expanded judicial review — works in the direction regulated industries want: it slows rulemaking and gives businesses more tools to contest protections whose benefits are diffuse and hard to price. The deadline suspensions are the clearest cost to the public; the disclosure of OMB communications is the clearest gain. On balance the bill's weight falls on the side of regulated interests, softened by the committee's amendments.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Governmental Affairs Committee held hearings, approved the bill with a substitute amendment, and reported it to the Senate calendar in May 1998, but Senate leadership never brought it up for a vote before the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Sen. Carl Levin introduced the bill in June 1997 with a bipartisan list of 15 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the Committee on Governmental Affairs.

The committee held hearings in September 1997 and February 1998, ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in March 1998, and reported it on May 11, 1998 with written report 105-188 — with additional and minority views filed.

The reported version, prepared under committee chair Sen. Fred Thompson, replaced the original text with a substitute that, among other changes, added required consideration of protections for sensitive subpopulations and state, local, and tribal input, and softened the judicial-review standard from 'clear and convincing' to the ordinary 'arbitrary or capricious' test.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on May 11, 1998, and no floor vote ever occurred before the Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one got the bill's changes. Health, safety, and environmental rulemaking continued under prior law without the new cost-benefit hurdles and deadline suspensions, which is the outcome public-interest opponents of the bill preferred; regulated industries, which stood to gain the litigation and delay tools, got nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 17 Republicans and 7 Democrats among 24 cosponsors, with a Democratic sponsor and a Republican committee chair — but opposition also ran across party lines, with committee Democrats filing minority views and public-interest groups, aligned with congressional Democrats, pushing to keep the bill off the floor.

industries.industry: Regulated manufacturers, energy producers, and other subjects of major federal rules
industries.note: The bill would hand these industries mandatory cost-benefit analysis, consideration of cheaper alternatives, suspended rule deadlines, and a richer court record for challenging rules — advantages that come directly at the expense of the timeliness and durability of public protections.

The bill explicitly excludes rules covering depository institutions, securities and commodities markets, and product approvals, shielding the financial sector from the new analysis regime while other industries face it. The public cost is indirect: financial rules would skip the transparency and analysis steps the bill imposes elsewhere.

The bill amends the Regulatory Flexibility Act to require five-year review plans for rules that significantly affect small entities, and requires agencies to evaluate flexible options and alternatives tailored to small businesses.
